title: Short Stuff: Mitsuye Endo
summary: Short Stuff episode on Mitsuye Endo, a natural-born American citizen and Sacramento-born state government secretary who was fired in 1942 under Executive Order 9066 along with other Japanese American state employees, then incarcerated in an internment camp. Attorney James C. Purcell took her case as a habeas corpus test case challenging the executive order. Endo agreed to proceed despite government offers to release her, and the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in her favor (Ex parte Endo). The ruling put pressure on Roosevelt, who ended the Japanese American internment camps the day before the decision was made public. Endo later moved to Chicago, worked for the Mayor's Committee on Race Relations, married Kenneth Sutsumi, raised three kids, and died of cancer in 2006. The hosts note the continuing debate over presidential wartime national security powers versus judicial checks.

segments.title: Introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode about Mitsuye Endo, a person in history who never got her due.

segments.title: Endo's background and firing
segments.summary: Endo was born in Sacramento, California, to Japanese immigrant parents, was a natural-born citizen, and worked as a secretary for the state Department of Employment. After Pearl Harbor and Executive Order 9066, the state fired all Japanese American state employees, including her.

segments.title: Lawsuit and incarceration
segments.summary: Sixty-three fired employees challenged the firings with backing from the Japanese American Citizens League and attorney James C. Purcell, who was not Japanese American. Endo's family was forcibly removed and she was incarcerated, eventually separated from her family and held in a detention center.

segments.title: Habeas corpus test case
segments.summary: Purcell sought a plaintiff for a habeas corpus petition. Endo was an ideal test case: a Methodist, a citizen, with a brother serving in the U.S. Army, who had never been to Japan. Despite cultural reluctance, she agreed after Purcell framed it as a case for all Japanese Americans.

segments.title: Supreme Court ruling and camp closures
segments.summary: The government offered to release Endo if she dropped the case; she refused and the case went to the Supreme Court, which unanimously ruled against the detention. The day before the decision was made public, Roosevelt announced the end of the internment camps, which the hosts say was driven by the looming ruling.

segments.title: Later life and legacy
segments.summary: Endo moved to Chicago, worked for the Mayor's Committee on Race Relations, married Kenneth Sutsumi, had three kids, and kept a low profile. She died of cancer in 2006. Law professor Amanda Tyler is cited on the case, and the hosts note the ongoing debate over presidential wartime power versus judicial review.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode, with Chuck suggesting Endo deserves a yearly parade.
